ListRow Svelte API

Issue 1648 implements the dense read-only form in ListRow.svelte, first consumed independently by HistoricalRunDetail.svelte and StageCard.svelte. name, art, tint and detail default to empty strings; icon defaults to fas fa-box. quantity is a caller-formatted string or number; null hides it and zero remains visible. tone accepts neutral (default), positive or danger; muted defaults false and draws a dashed edge with subdued name. Optional trailing supplies inline contextual evidence such as a chance chip. truncateName=false preserves wrapping; true ellipsizes name and detail on one line, retaining full DOM/title text. Journal hosts use four equal tracks for materials, awards and reusable tools, whose detail names each stage’s quantity/state rather than summing consumption. No lookup or quantity inference occurs here.

Selectable form — issue 1778, first drawn by the Journal’s Active runs (RunCard.svelte), then by the gathering environments, tasks and events (EnvironmentCard.svelte, GatheringTaskRow.svelte, GatheringEventRow.svelte) at the default density, each leading with its own 64px or 56px thumb, and a locked environment drawn as the inert form; then by the crafting browser’s recipe rows (RecipeListRow.svelte) at the default density, leading with a 38px thumbnail that carries the uncraftable pip, with the favourite and cart buttons trailing and an uncraftable recipe on the danger tone; then by the alchemy known recipes and components (KnownRecipesColumn.svelte, ComponentInventoryColumn.svelte) at the default density with a 38px mark, and the alchemy discipline chooser’s cards (AlchemyDisciplineChooser.svelte) at the card layout; then by the inventory grid’s cards (InventoryItemCard.svelte) at the card layout, each leading with its fluid square thumbnail over its name on one ellipsized line, the whole name in its title, Shift selecting several, a broken item on the danger tone, and the essence editor’s preview of a card drawn as the inert form. density dense (the default; the selectable form insets space-1/space-2 with a space-1 line gap) | default (radius 11, space-3/space-4) · layout row | card, the merged browse card below · markSize 22, 26, 30 or 38, each a literal rung of the art-tile ladder, any other value warning and drawing 22 · inset form (the default) | row, which gives the dense selectable form the dense row’s space-2/space-3 inset so it stands the height of a read-only dense row, inert at the default density, on the card layout and on a row drawing no selectable form (issue 2321) · detailAlign start (the default, the 50% detail column) | end, which holds a truncated row’s detail at its trailing edge, at most 40% of the row, in the muted ink (issue 2321) · bodyBasis auto (the default) | fill, which gives a form’s body flex: 1 1 0, so a reading set under the name wraps inside it and the trailing figures keep the first flex line (issue 2257, YieldScale’s rows) · leading replaces the mark · badges inline after the name, wrapping, where truncateName keeps them on the name’s line until the name would narrow past 6ch · meta · children · aside · selected, where undefined is an action row with no pressed state · disabled · onOpen(event) · openProps · nameClass. With onOpen the content is ONE native <button type="button" data-keyboard-focus="true"> holding phrasing content only, pressed while selected is given and true; openProps alone draws an inert div, and with neither there is no wrapper. openProps lands on that control: a key the control owns (type, role, tabindex, aria-pressed, disabled, data-keyboard-focus, and any onclick handler) is dropped, its class follows fabricate-list-row-open, and its aria-describedby follows the meta, children and aside ids. Its aria-label is the item’s name followed by every state the row only draws. trailing holds real controls beside the button and aside holds block content beneath it, both outside it, and the form draws leading and trailing inside wrappers of its own, so a caller’s root keeps its own positioning; the button’s ::after covers the row, so the row opens it from anywhere but a trailing control, while the button’s own content stays above it for its titles and tooltips. Selection is drawn from aria-pressed as the --fab-surface-active fill behind the --fab-accent-border edge, the multi-select rule; a danger row keeps its own ground and takes a 1px inset ring. With no form prop the dense output is unchanged. ListRow is shipped, by the maintainer’s 2026-10-12 ruling (epic 1495); the planned-migrations row “List row geometry” records that these specimens were redrawn to the shipped forms (issues 1523 and 2547).

ListState API
  • SHIPPED — built at issue 2548 as components/ListState.svelte and read here from its $props(), to the two browse list units above: a list’s loading and error forms, which replace the list’s body and leave its header in place. Its three importers are SystemsBrowserView.svelte, EnvironmentsBrowserView.svelte and KnowledgeRoster.svelte; a list that loads together with its view takes PlayerViewState instead.
  • Props: loading, default false, which masks the error and the body · loadingLabel, already localized and required while loading, because the status line states what is loading · skeletonRows, a whole number from 1 to 6, default 3, any other value drawing 3 · density default | dense, the selectable ListRow density the rows preview, any other value reading default · error, the already-localized notice title, where '' is no error; DataTable’s error is the message, and this one is the title · errorDetail, optional plain text beneath the title, rendered escaped and never as markup · children, the ready body.
  • Passthrough: no class and no rest spread, because the component has no single root. loadingProps and errorProps carry data-* hooks only, onto the loading region and onto the notice: any other key is dropped, as is an error key starting data-notice-, which Notice reserves for its own hooks, so a caller cannot override the region’s class or busy state or the notice’s role or tone, and a true value writes an empty one, so a presence selector matches it.
  • Rendering: loading masks error, and error masks the body. Loading is one region carrying aria-busy="true", holding a status line at 11.5px in --fab-text-muted over the skeleton rows, which are static because the motion rule animates nothing; each row stands the selectable ListRow’s frame, inset and border-box height at its density, its mark and bars on --fab-border-strong. The error is a danger Notice carrying the title and detail, non-blocking as the view-state composition’s error branch is, because a list failing beside a usable header is not an interruption. Ready renders the body with no element around it, so a caller’s child rules still reach its markup.
  • Accessible naming: the visible status line states what is loading and carries role="status", and the region carries only aria-busy; the skeleton rows are aria-hidden and hold nothing focusable, and the error notice is announced by its role on insertion, as every Notice is.
Card layout, the merged browse card
  • MERGED — issue 1778 merged <BrowseCard> into ListRow’s layout="card" (its decision D2): the card-grid unit above is the same row model on one track, so a browse card is a <ListRow layout="card"> and no second component. The alchemy discipline chooser (AlchemyDisciplineChooser.svelte) draws it first, a 38px mark above the name, its count as meta and its blurb and enter cue as children.
  • Props: ListRow’s own. name · art, icon and tint, resolved by the caller and drawn as the 38px mark (markSize={38}) · meta the ordered facts beneath the name, each already localized · selected · disabled. It takes no track or column prop: the grid belongs to the list around it, and a card that could set its own width is how four widths happened.
  • Event contract: onOpen — the whole card is the control, so there is no separate open affordance to place. It draws no select box of its own: a browse grid that needs multi-selection uses the ROW form, which has somewhere to put one. The inventory grid is the one exception (issue 1778, decision E2): its cards keep Shift selection, each selected card pressed and marked by a check in its thumbnail, because the grid already reads as a grid of owned items and its multi-selection was shipped there.
  • Accessible naming: the card is a button whose accessible name is the record’s name; the mark is decorative, and selected, when given, is announced as the button’s pressed state rather than by the border alone. A card that only acts, as the chooser’s do, takes no selected and so no pressed state.
ViewToggle API
  • SHIPPED — built at issue 2412 as components/ViewToggle.svelte and read here from its $props(), to the switcher drawn above, which is the essence browser’s list and grid switcher at its icon-only form. With that one importer, EssenceBrowserView.svelte, it is recorded as a non-member on the LogList, StageNav and XrefList precedent.
  • Props: view list | grid, a CLOSED set of two, because a third arrangement is a different screen rather than a third button, and anything other than grid reads as list · listLabel and gridLabel, both required, since each control renders a glyph and nothing else. It IS <SegmentedControl iconOnly>, composed rather than restated: the two glyph controls are its options and those two labels are the options’ own, view is its value, and the group label is its ariaLabel. EssenceBrowserView.svelte renders it. optionDataAttr names the per-option hook, written on each option’s clickable label and never on its radio.
  • Geometry: segments are 32.4px wide in Foundry, where Font Awesome draws its glyph in a 1.25em box.
  • Passthrough: class plus a rest spread on the root, written after the class and before the fixed track props, so a caller cannot override them — the spread carries the data-* hook a harness or a capture step selects on, so the attribute is genuinely absent when unset.
  • Event contract: onChange receives the chosen view, forwarded from the segmented control’s own. It holds no state of its own: the list around it owns which arrangement is current, so a toggle and its grid cannot disagree.
  • Accessible naming: a radio group with its own required label, and the two glyph controls are its radios — the segmented control’s rule, since exactly one of two named options is chosen at all times. Each radio’s name is its label prop; neither is derived from the glyph.
XrefList API
  • SHIPPED — built at issue 2321 as components/XrefList.svelte and read here from its $props(), to the dense unit above, which is the cross-reference form: a kicker, then rows at a 22px mark, a 12px semibold name and an inline quantity, at radius 9. A cross-reference list is a read-only list that states which records a record relates to: what uses it, what produces it, what it is required for, who holds it or what contributes to it. It is not import-export’s stored cross-reference, which is a persisted reference between documents, and a list whose rows carry actions, or open a body in place, is not one. Its first callers are the player inventory inspector’s Sources, Contributing, Used by, Required for and Produced by sections, all in InventoryComponentDetail.svelte; with that one importer it is recorded as a non-member on the LogList and StageNav precedent, and the manager’s cross-reference lists are adoption debt under issue 2322.
  • Props: label the kicker above the list, required and already localized · items an ordered list, each a name, a mark and an optional caller-formatted quantity. Each row IS the dense <ListRow>, or its selectable dense form for a row that opens, composed rather than restated, so a change to that row reaches every cross-reference in the app; every row is one ellipsized line, 40px border-box whether it opens or not. Four item extensions: id, the row’s key, its position when absent · detail, the caller-formatted role or kind, drawn at the row’s trailing edge in the muted ink and never as a quantity · opens: false, which keeps that row from being a control in a list given onOpen · attrs, spread on that row’s root, because Required for and Produced by need two hook names with different values. With zero items it draws the label and no list: the caller owns the empty state and the pager beneath it.
  • Passthrough: class plus a rest spread on the root, written after the class — the spread carries the data-* hook a harness or a capture step selects on, so the attribute is genuinely absent when unset.
  • Event contract: onOpen, optional, receives the item as passed — a list without it renders rows that are not controls at all, which is the read-only inspector case, and with it every row whose opens is not false is ListRow’s one native button, never pressed, which links out. It has no remove and no reorder: a cross-reference states a relationship and is never where that relationship is edited.
  • Accessible naming: a list named by its own kicker; a row that opens is a button named by its text, the item’s name followed by its detail and quantity, and a row that does not open holds nothing focusable. The quantity and the detail are text, so a multiple or a role is never carried by colour or position alone.

Canonical spec
  • selection bar the LAST row of the browser’s toolbar, directly above its list, on a top hairline with an 8px pad and no fill: tri-state page box and a muted 600 “Select all”, a 1×16 divider, the accent 700 count with its glyph, the info-ink “Select all N results” link, and a subtle trailing Clear
  • panel replaces the inspector: an accent kicker beside Clear selection, an accent-soft hero (radius 10, a 36×36 radius-9 tile, a serif 700 count over a muted hint), then the staged axes; fields default to “leave unchanged” and only touched fields write

  • dock the panel’s dock is an <InspectorPanel> foot (issue 2500), so it bleeds by and paints its scroller’s own --fab-manager-inspector-pad and --fab-manager-inspector-bg: the panel’s own fill, on a top hairline
  • blocked rows listed with their reason before the write, inside a warning notice above the dock; Apply counts only the rows it writes to
  • report after the write, a notice states what changed and lists what was skipped, in place of the forecast
  • delete arms in the dock, under Apply, and states impact — a named carve-out from the dialog default

Svelte API
  • SHIPPED — read from BulkSelectionToolbar.svelte and BulkEditPanelShell.svelte’s $props() at issue 1782.
  • the bar — pageSelectionState none | some | all · count · showSelectAllResults · selectAllResultsCount · selectAllScope results | shown
  • onTogglePage · onSelectAllResults · onClear
  • selectAllLabel · hint — pre-localized strings, empty by default so the studios render unchanged
  • trailingActions · bareActions · countIcon — three recorded departures from the reference, each opt-in
  • rowClass · toolbarAttr · pageBoxAttr · countAttr · resultsAttr · clearAttr — the data-* hooks per studio
  • the panel — heading · applyLabel · canApply — applyLabel is the studio’s: the shell’s own default, used when it is empty, is noun-free (“Apply to {count}”), and the studio supplies the noun, as this drawing’s “Apply to 3 essences” does · clearLabel · hint pre-localized overrides · onClearSelection · onApply · children and dockFoot snippets · panelAttr · clearAttr · countAttr · applyAttr
  • subjectCount number — the records the selection names; Apply writes to it less the blocked rows, and names that count when applyLabel is empty; when every named record is blocked Apply is inert and reads “Nothing to apply”. Unset, Apply follows canApply and applyLabel alone and the notice reads “{count} cannot be changed”. Relocated from <SetPicker> at issue 1513: the record count belongs to the panel that COMMITS, and the staging inset the panel wraps stages without writing.
  • blocked {id, reason}[] — the rows Apply will skip, listed inside the notice. Each reason is already localized and names its own row: id is only a data hook and is never shown, so a bare “locked compendium” tells the GM nothing. Ids need not be unique.
  • report {changed, skipped?} | null — what the last Apply actually changed, rendered in place of the blocked forecast. Success only when every record changed; a skip, a shortfall or a zero-change write is a warning, and a skip is counted in the title. It has no dismiss on purpose: it persists until the caller clears it.
  • The sketch this replaced owned the SELECTION as data (selected id[] bindable, total). The pair takes a count and callbacks instead, so the selection lives in the caller’s model.
The reasons ride the Notice evidence band (issue 1648). The blocked and skipped lists render through Notice’s evidence() snippet, so each shares its notice’s edge and fill and takes the band’s 11px mono secondary ink; Notice has no free-form children slot. No caller passes subjectCount, blocked or report yet; the View Lab specimen manager-bulk-edit-panel-shell-specimen photographs the three states from the real shell.

The Essence Rules browser is the exemplar, and issue 1782 redrew this specimen from its bar and its Icon, Colour and Status panel rather than repainting any bulk screen. The earlier sketch drew the bar as an accent-soft band carrying Edit and Delete verbs and the panel as a plain card with Cancel; none of those ships, because the panel opens on selection and delete arms inside it.

  • query · onQuery(next) · placeholder — the well; page · onPage(index) — a pageBulkInsetRows result and the pager’s request
  • empty · hasRows · disabled · rowsDisabled · max · minRows · children snippet for a caller that draws its own rows
Why the rows are the inset’s. A snippet rendered as children carries the scope of the component that defines it, so the row family is painted by the primitive under :global() rooted at its own root, and a caller that hands rows and a kind gets the reference’s row without writing one. The two panels then differ only in data sources and write targets, which is what the maintainer asked for. Why the row carries a third state. A two-state box cannot distinguish “remove this from all twelve” from “leave this one alone”, so the tri row cycles add → remove → leave unchanged and unchecking can never silently strip membership from a record the GM never meant to touch. It is ONE CYCLING CONTROL rather than a three-way segmented control because the row is a list entry in a scrolling window, and a segmented control per row spends the row’s whole width on a control the GM reads rather than operates. The count the commit writes to belongs to the panel that commits, not here: this inset stages and does not write.2 callers · BulkStagingInset.svelte · ComponentBulkEditPanel.svelte, ComponentCatalogueBulkPanel.svelte

When a table, and when a list. Reach for this only when a reader compares the same field DOWN a column — a date, an amount, a name. A record with a portrait, a status and two actions is a <ListRow>; forcing it into columns costs the art and the affordances and buys nothing. The tell is whether the columns would be worth sorting.

Three controls, three jobs. A toggle is independently on or off and any combination is valid. A segmented is one-of-N and the list is always in one of them — a scope, not a filter you can clear. A select is one-of-many where the options are data. A segmented that could be "none" is a toggle in disguise.

Both shipped rungs are on the portrait ladder, and the art-size ratchet holds every Avatar site to it.
  • shape round (a person) or square (a party, a vehicle or a place) — a CLOSED set, caller-supplied for the reason the caption states. round is the default because the person mark is the reading a caller gets wrong by silence.
  • tint a bare --fab-tag-* palette key. Unset is byte-identical to a flat tile, because the 30% mix and the ring are CLASS-GATED rather than written as values: an unset custom property inside a color-mix() on the base rule makes the declaration invalid at computed-value time and the tile loses its ground entirely. The ring RECOLOURS the border rather than adding a shadow, so a tinted tile and an untinted one still align in a roster.
  • TARGET — none, and no class, no style and no rest spread. IMPORT-FREE LEAF: one util import inside a leaf propagates a required raw-module entry into every mount harness compiling anything that renders it, and a missing entry HANGS that suite rather than failing it. It also does NOT compare against the system’s own default artwork — the fallback trigger is the caller’s, per the note below.
Rail API
  • SHIPPED — built at issue 1782 as components/Rail.svelte and read here from its $props(), with the first unit above re-derived to the shipped exemplar, the essence inspector: a bare column at --fab-space-2 opened by a kicker in <Kicker>’s muted ink with a 2px foot, which no caller restyles (issue 2257). It is ONE SECTION of a right-hand inspector column — never the column itself, never the nav rail’s block and never <NavSidebar>’s icon variant. Three inspectors draw it: the essence browser inspector, the tool rules inspector’s two groups, and the recipe-item editor’s preview rail.
  • Props: label the section’s kicker, already localized · children its body · class an EXTRA class, appended after the primitive’s own fab-rail. It declares no width: the column is a track of the caller’s grid, so a rail that set its own would fight the page it sits in.
  • Passthrough: a rest spread on the root, written after the naming — the spread carries the data-* hook a harness or a capture step selects on, so the attribute is genuinely absent when unset.
  • Event contract: none, and this is the convention the caption states rather than an omission — a rail shows consequences and links out, and never hosts an editing input. A verb or a link inside it is the caller’s own control and carries its own handler.
  • Accessible naming: a labelled section is a group named by its kicker, so a reader moving between sections hears what each one answers; an unlabelled one is an unnamed <section>. Neither is a region, because a column of named landmarks would bury the screen’s own.
LogList API
  • SHIPPED — built at issue 1782 as components/LogList.svelte and read here from its $props(), with the second unit above re-derived to the shipped exemplar, the journal’s Finished list, so no converted frame moves. That list is its one caller: the journal’s recent-results rows this entry first cited no longer render, because RecentResults.svelte has no importer. The time is the type ladder’s mono log line, 9.5px in --fab-text-muted, ellipsized on overflow with the whole time as its title; a hovered entry’s raised ground takes it to --fab-text-secondary, and each ink clears 4.5:1 on the ground it is drawn on (issue 2257).
  • Props: entries an ordered list, each a key, a text, a caller-formatted when string, an optional art path drawn as the 26px icon chip, a tone whose danger grounds the row in that family, an optional outcome mark of icon, label, tone and props, and props, attributes spread on the entry’s open control. The time is caller-formatted because a tick count, a world date and a real duration are three different sentences · ariaLabel the list’s name, already localized · selectedKey the open entry’s key · action a snippet handed each entry and drawn beside its open control, never inside it: the journal’s dismiss · class an EXTRA class, appended after the primitive’s own fab-log-list.
  • Passthrough: a rest spread on the root, written after the class — the spread carries the data-* hook a harness or a capture step selects on, so the attribute is genuinely absent when unset.
  • Event contract: onOpen, optional, receives the entry on a click, Enter or Space — the journal opens a run from its line, and a list without it renders inert entries with no control and nothing in the tab order.
  • Accessible naming: a list named by its required ariaLabel, each entry a listitem; an openable entry is a button, pressed while it is the selected one, and an outcome is an image named by its label, so a success and a failure are told apart without colour.
TierTrack API
  • SHIPPED — read from components/TierTrack.svelte’s $props() at issue 2424, which built it, with the third and fourth units above drawn to it. A DISCRETE ladder: neither <RangeBar>’s continuous axis nor a <Meter>. Its row badges are Chip, and it is published through game.fabricate.api.ui, which the premium companion’s player faction ladder draws it through; its one caller is the seam’s runtime adapter, so it is a non-member with one caller.
  • Props: tiers each { id?, name, figure?, notes?, valence? } in drawn order, figure and notes drawn in column only; a non-array draws empty and a tier that is not a plain object is skipped but keeps its index · currentIndex an index into tiers as passed, where anything not an in-range integer reaches nothing · direction ascending or descending (highest first) · layout row or column, an unknown value of either reading its default · ariaLabel, currentLabel, reachedLabel and aheadLabel, REQUIRED and already localized · hint a caller-formatted sentence beneath the track · class declared for Fabricate’s own callers and not published.
  • Valence: a tier’s valence is positive, negative or neutral; an absent one reads positive and any other value neutral. Position decides which tiers are reached, and valence colours only a reached tier’s mark, so an unreached tier can never read as reached. In row a reached tier’s badge takes Chip’s tone of the same name, and neutral takes Chip’s secondary; in column an ahead dot is a hollow ring. The current tier is reached and keeps its valence, marked by a location-pin glyph in row and by its visible currentLabel and an accent edge in column. A tier’s valence restates what its name already says and is never the only carrier of it: it is drawn in colour alone and reaches no assistive technology.
  • Passthrough: a rest spread on the root <div>, written after the class — the spread carries the data-* hook a harness or a capture step selects on, so the attribute is genuinely absent when unset.
  • Event contract: none. A ladder is stated, not operated; the tier a record sits at is a consequence of its own figures.
  • Accessible naming: an ordered list with an explicit role="list", named by ariaLabel; the current tier carries aria-current="step" and currentLabel, every other tier its visually hidden reachedLabel or aheadLabel after its name, and the chevrons, dots and glyph are decorative because the order is the list’s own.
The initials fallback is rare, not routine. Core assigns default artwork on creation, so an actor is never art-less — the fallback triggers only when the component compares against the system's own default. And the redaction-safe DTO carries no tint and no kind, so both are caller-supplied too.src/bootstrap/Fabricate.js — listCraftingSourceActors, the redaction-safe actor DTO
Rare, and REACHABLE as of issue 1514. The note above is right about creation — Core assigns default artwork, so an actor is never art-less — and the state it calls unreachable is drawn at two of the portrait’s four shipped call sites now. Each is a projection rather than an actor: the crafting tab’s two source-actor sites pass the EMPTY STRING when the projection resolves no image, and this component renders initials for anything falsy without comparing against a default-artwork constant. Both drew <i class="fas fa-user"> before, so the conversion is a CONTENT change as well as a frame move, and it is UNPHOTOGRAPHABLE: every View Lab actor carries a portrait, so no frame can draw it and mounted assertions are what hold it. The portrait sits on the mount harnesses’ shared-primitive list, and shape is mandatory at both, because the default is round and each of these wells has always drawn a rounded square.tests/avatar-source-contract.test.js pins the census at four call sites, all passing art

A result amount is either a fixed positive integer or a rolled expression, and the row toggles between them in place. A requirement amount is always fixed and the ingredient row offers no toggle: a rolled requirement has no coherent moment to resolve — at craft time it fails a crafter holding two against a 1d4 that came up three, and at read time it either changes under the reader or means nothing. A result has one unambiguous moment, the award. The rolled form takes dice plus optional actor data paths. It shows no resolved value: authoring a recipe has no previewed actor, so a number here would be fiction and the space is better spent on the expression. The toggle is not a third quantity kind — it selects which control occupies the quantity slot, so the row keeps one meaning and one position for the amount.

There is no “result” kind. One row and one choice group serve both sides; the context decides which kinds the select offers. Component and currency appear on both. Tag and essence are ingredient-only, because each describes a class of thing to consume and a craft cannot produce a class. The shipped ingredient side offers component, currency, essence and tag; a recipe's non-progressive result set offers component, currency and recipe knowledge (issue 1773), and a progressive set, a gathering task and salvage offer component alone.

Every standalone row carries “or…”, immediately before the remove action, because any requirement can become a choice group. Only rows already inside a group drop it — the group carries its own Alternative adder.

The lead chip carries the kind’s tint. Tag is purple throughout: the chips, the lead, the adder and the Any-of / All-of control, which is right-aligned with the quantity rather than trailing the run. Tag is the one abstract kind — it matches any item carrying a value rather than naming a record.

A tag row holds several tags, so it has no subject cell. It carries a run of removable chips and a dashed adder that opens the tag catalogue; the tag is the value, so there is nothing for a subject cell to name. No word leads the run: the right-aligned control states how the tags match, at every tag count.

A unit belongs to the right of the stepper, never under the name. Currency has one; an essence amount does not.

Svelte API

  • onChange required

ChoiceGroup ships in two forms
  • The ingredient form: a bordered set of picker rows under a header pill.
  • The result form: the same box under the award header — strategy, N, repeats, then the chooser Segmented — with a range cell per rolled alternative; the three entries below.
  • The two-tint rule survives as guidance on PickerRow.
The chooser is the result side’s one addition, and it is a Segmented, not a toggle — both values are live behaviour, and neither is the absence of the other. It sits in the group header, not on the rows, because it governs the whole bundle.

Switching it changes which controls the rows carry. Rolled reveals the selection expression in the header and a range cell per alternative; player-chooses hides both, because a range with no roll behind it is authoring that cannot fire. The rows are the same <PickerRow> in both states — only the range cell appears and disappears.

The selection expression is the group’s own roll, not the craft’s check, and it resolves against the crafting character. A roll outside every authored range clamps to the nearest one rather than reporting a gap: a craft routed this far still awards something.

An ingredient-side group never shows it. The crafter is always the one deciding what to spend, so the control would offer a choice the model does not have. It is one of exactly two documented differences between the two containers’ groups; the award strategy below is the other.spec.md requirement "A result-side choice group states who chooses and how many it awards"
A repeated draw is not a third strategy. It is up to N under a roll with repeats allowed — the same count, the same ceiling, one setting apart — so the closed set is two and the matrix has no cell left to forbid.

Up to N is a ceiling, not a quota — fewer is a legal outcome, and a two-alternative group set to up-to-three is authored rather than invalid. Without repeats, an N above the alternative count exhausts the bundle rather than erroring; with repeats allowed the pool never runs out and N is exact.

Repeats belong to up to N under a roll alone. Any one of has nothing to repeat and a player picking from a visible list cannot repeat, so the setting is absent in the other three cells.

The header reads as one sentence — award strategy, N, repeats, chooser, left to right — with the help line restating the resolved behaviour in prose. Four controls in a row are read faster as a sentence than as a form.
Not under progressive. Progressive walks an ordered result list against a check-value budget and awards every entry the roll affords, so neither the chooser nor the award strategy has anything to mean there and the surface offers neither. The other four modes route to exactly one result set, and what a group inside it awards is a within-group concern.

A container-level group adder is ruled out. An “Add variable set” button next to “Add result” creates an empty group, asking the GM to state what the alternatives are before stating what the first one replaces, and it leaves two paths to one construct. A set’s adders create rows; a group is always something an existing row became.spec.md requirement "A result-side choice group states who chooses and how many it awards"
The offered kinds belong to the surface, not to the row. A downtime activity offers component, currency and recipe knowledge — a patron can teach as well as pay. A gathering task offers component, and currency once gathering currency ships: it hands over material the character carried back, and neither recipe knowledge nor an advanced craft is something a wilderness task can produce. The kind select, the convert menu and the adders state the same subset.

One adder, named for what it adds. Alternative inside a choice group, Ingredient in an ingredient set, Result in a result set — and it opens the same kind menu the convert control opens. Naming the adders after the kinds instead would state the menu’s list twice.
An alternative inside a choice group is this same row. It carries the kind select, the searched value, the Fixed / Rolled amount switch and the currency naming body exactly as a standalone row does — only the convert control is replaced, by the range cell when the group is rolled. A group member that drops the amount toggle has omitted the amount’s own control; one that drops the body leaves a currency alternative unnameable.
The convert control and the group’s own “Alternative” adder open the SAME menu — the offered kinds, in the same order — and both append an empty row of the chosen kind. A convert that silently prefills a second alternative has answered a question the GM was about to be asked.spec.md requirement "One requirement row serves both sides of a recipe"

  • commit ‘staged’ | ‘choose’ = ‘staged’
  • onChange(next, {added, removed}) required
  • maxTokens number = 3 — tokens before the overflow count

  • trigger snippet — replaces the dashed Add · class · rest
Why it is not just a multi-select popover. Three obligations the search popover does not carry: the trigger is bounded, so a record in forty books renders four tokens and a count rather than forty; selection is staged and applied on commit, so a mis-click costs nothing and Clear is always reachable; and the panel states matched-of-total beside its search, so a GM knows when to refine the query rather than keep scrolling. The MULTI-RECORD edit is NOT one of them: the third state a staged bulk edit needs moved to <BulkStagingInset> at issue 1513, which ships it. Used by: the recipe-item editor’s contents tab (staged) · the crafting component sources bar (choose, the session control).Book membership is stored as recipeIds on the book, so the same control drives both directions of the relation

Three rules the expanded row depends on. The row is a <li> and the disclosure is the only button in it that OPENS the row: a whole-row button nests the delete control, which is invalid DOM that createElement accepts and no mounted test notices. Disclosure and drag state are local to the list and keyed by record id, so they survive the store refresh that follows every persisted edit — lift them to the store and a row collapses under the GM mid-edit. And alwaysOpen is a real mode rather than a caller convenience: on a tab whose entire subject is the body, a single-expand accordion defaults to showing nothing.RecipeStepAccordion.svelte header and its alwaysOpen prop · ComplicationSummaryRow.svelte (4 call sites) · RowDisclosure.svelte
RULED: a collapsed body STAYS in the DOM. The maintainer ruled KEEP, and section 16 carries the row. The body is retained under display:none with hidden and inert, so its controls leave the tab order with it: one markup tree rather than a second rendering path, and retention holds the uncommitted field state that unmounting discards. It is ONE switch in this component with no prop exposing it, because a choice offered per call site is how two defensible behaviours became accidental — the step accordion and the complication row both used to unmount, the Checks Studio trigger card kept it, and nobody had decided. A whole-header row outside this list is not yet bound by the rule and that debt is recorded as a non-conformance rather than as a conforming case.maintainer, 2026-09-18 · design-system/spec.md (the ordered-row requirement) · SortableList.svelte · sortable-list-mounted.test.js

ExprInput API
  • SHIPPED — read from RollDataExpressionInput.svelte’s $props() at issue 2465.
  • Props: value the expression, rendered in the mono field · tokens the ordered insertable tokens, drawn as dashed 26px buttons in the mono face in a row beneath the field that wraps, a token ellipsizing only where it alone is wider than its host · tokensLabel the token group’s accessible name, required with tokens and never defaulted · resolve a caller-supplied synchronous function from the expression to a number or null, ABSENT where no actor is in scope — the resolver and its roll data are the caller’s, and no reading is drawn without it; it is never called for a blank expression, and a result that is not a finite number, or a resolver that throws, reads as null · unresolvedLabel the caller’s short statement that the expression does not reduce, drawn trimmed, required with resolve and never defaulted; where it is blank, an expression that does not reduce draws no reading · placeholder, empty by default · disabled the field and every token inert together. It reads no game state of its own.
  • Reading: drawn first in the row beneath the field, ahead of the tokens, on every change of the expression or the resolver: a number as = {n} through the chip’s info tone at inspector density in the mono face, written as the resolver returned it; the caller’s statement through its secondary tone in the UI face where the expression does not reduce; nothing for a blank expression. The reading is never truncated: a statement wraps inside its chip and a number is written whole.
  • Passthrough: class plus a rest spread on the input, written after the class — the spread carries the data-* hook a harness or a capture step selects on, so the attribute is genuinely absent when unset. Here it also carries the input’s name, description and invalid state, which the caller holds. The component writes its reading’s id ahead of that description.
  • Event contract: onChange receives the whole expression, and it fires for a typed edit and for a token alike — a token inserts AT THE CURSOR rather than at the end, which with the resolver is the behaviour nothing else in the set owns and the reason this is a primitive where bounds and currency inputs are compositions. A token replaces a partial selection, and joins the end when the whole expression is selected or the caret or an edge of the selection stands inside a term; it takes a + on either side where an operand stands there and none beside an operator, a bracket or a comma, and hands focus back to the field with the caret after it; onChange fires once for it, with the expression’s outer whitespace trimmed.
  • Accessible naming: the field is a real input named by the shared field shell’s kicker where that shell is a <label>, and otherwise by the caller’s aria-labelledby or aria-label on the spread, each token is a button whose text is its own name, in a group named by tokensLabel that holds the tokens alone, never the reading; the reading describes the field; and one visually hidden status region beside the row, mounted with resolve and empty until an edit, speaks the reading once typing has settled for 500ms, or once focus has returned to the field after a token, and only where the edit changed it — including the case where it does not reduce to a number, which is stated rather than left blank, and a reading that changes because the resolver did is not spoken. A caller that passes tokens or resolve must host the field outside a <label>, which would otherwise take every token, the reading and the status region’s text into the field’s name.

Four states, distinguished at a glance before any caption is read. Met is a hairline ring outside the tile and a success pip inked --fab-on-success. Short is a danger ring, a danger pip inked --fab-on-danger and danger caption ink — it is stated, never hidden, because knowing what you are missing is what sends a player out to find it. Partial is a partly delivered essence, a to-do rather than a shortfall: a --fab-warning-border ring, a pip on solid --fab-warning inked --fab-bg-0 and --fab-warning-text caption ink. No on-warning ink is declared, so the pip takes the page ground as every solid warning chip does (6.4:1 to 13.4:1 across the shipped themes); --fab-warning-text on that ground would read about 1.1:1. It is never painted short, even while the solver still reports the group missing. Open is a dashed accent frame, an empty ring inked --fab-accent-text, a pip carrying how many candidates the slot offers rather than a held-versus-needed count that does not exist yet, and a small affordance line under the caption. The tile the player has opened takes the accent outline, which is the same selection mark the chooser family uses, and a tick at its corner, so a pressed tile never reads as focus alone. A pressed tile always opens its candidates directly beneath the row, so it is never drawn without its list. The count pill sits on a solid ground, never a wash, because it is read over art of unknown colour.
a pressed tile under keyboard focus — the pressed outline thickens to a 4px band

The module focus ring is the same 2px accent outline at offset 2 that a pressed tile already draws, so on its own it would change nothing. A pressed tile that holds keyboard focus therefore thickens that outline to a 4px accent band flush with the tile, which follows its radius and stays inside the 4px gap above the caption. The accent clears 3:1 on --fab-bg-0, --fab-bg-1, --fab-surface and --fab-bg-2 in all seven themes. It is drawn by hand here because a live specimen cannot hold keyboard focus.
a slot with several candidates — the tile counts them, it never summarises them
Any binder 1 of 3
Any hardwood 1 of 12
Any solvent 2 of 2
Pine Resin change
A 56px tile has room for one number, so an unfilled slot spends it on how many candidates there are and nothing else. It does not attempt a held-versus-needed count — there are three of those to report and no candidate has been chosen — and it does not try to summarise the candidates themselves, which is precisely what the option list beneath the row is for. The caption names what the slot is for rather than a component, because no component is in it yet, and the affordance line carries how many the player must pick of how many offered: 1 of 3, or 2 of 2 where the requirement takes two.

The slash is the whole distinction. A pip with a slash is always held over needed, on its semantic ground — success when met, warning when partly delivered, danger when short. A pip with no slash is always how many candidates, on the accent ground, and is only ever seen on an unfilled slot. The moment a candidate is chosen the tile switches to the slashed form, takes the component’s own name and art, and its affordance line becomes change. Two number shapes, two grounds, one meaning each — and no tile ever carries both.

An essence tile obeys the same one-number rule. With a single threshold it shows that threshold’s got/need; with several it shows pools met over pools required — 1/2 — because a tile cannot carry a pair of numbers per essence. The per-essence figures live in the pool panel, which has the width for them.
the open slot’s candidates — one 44px row each, in flow beneath

The list is in flow, not floating: it is the answer to the tile directly above it, and a popover would cover the row the player is comparing against. Each candidate states held, needed and spare in mono — the numbers the decision turns on. Duskglass is dimmed, disabled and gives its reason: the player holds two, but this stage has already claimed both for its essence pool, so none is spare — the ONE case a candidate is disabled. Bone Ash is held short of the need, which is different: it is still offered with its chip and name dimmed, its reading in danger ink at full opacity, so it keeps 4.5:1, and that reading describes it through aria-describedby, because knowing what almost works is what sends a player to find one more. A candidate that cannot be used is shown and explained rather than omitted. The list is ONE single-select radiogroup: one tab stop, on the checked candidate or else the first offered one, and the arrows, Home and End move the focus and the choice together, passing over a disabled candidate. One slot is open at a time, and the row above stays visible while it is.

  • SlotTile: label · ariaLabel · art / icon (the open face defaults to the empty ring fa-regular fa-circle) / tint · state met | partial | short | open · pip caller-formatted · pipKind ratio | candidate · affordance · interactive · pressed · disabled · onActivate

Spare stock, not held stock, decides whether a candidate is usable. One stage can claim the same component from three directions at once — a fixed quantity, an open slot, and an essence source list — and all three are claims on one pile. Every cap, every disabled increment and every dimmed candidate is derived from a single claims map for the stage, so the row can never offer a component it has already spent elsewhere in the same stage. A design that checks held per requirement lets a player double-spend and only discovers it on commit.
Each fact lives in exactly one place. The stage being worked shows its live slot row and states only its output; the countdown belongs to the time card, the state to the stage’s own tag, and the blocker to the line under the progress kicker. Restating any of them beside the tiles gives two surfaces the chance to disagree, which is how a player stops trusting either.
All three converge on the specimen at issue 2257 (ruling 2026-10-07; D13, D16). Issue 1648 task 6 supplied the components and their mounted chooser contract, and issue 1644 measured them on their override frames. SlotTile draws its met, short and partial edge as a 1px ring outside the 56 tile, declared per state because the open face draws its dashed border instead; its pip is 16.4 tall at line-height 1.6; and a pressed tile keeps its tick, now drawn above. The partial and candidate pips take --fab-bg-0, while the met and short pips keep --fab-on-success and --fab-on-danger, because --fab-bg-0 measures 3.70:1 on foundry-native’s success and 4.48:1 on ironblood-forge’s danger (maintainer, 2026-10-10); the specimen’s met and short pips and its 3px affordance gap are redrawn to the shipped tile. SlotRow names the row with the shared <Kicker> and sets its hint at k-hint’s 1.5. ChoiceOptionList marks each candidate with the borderless 26 Medallion chip at radius 7 with an 11px glyph, in the option’s tint, else accent, sets its summary at 1.5, and dims a short candidate’s chip and name only: the whole-candidate .6 the specimen drew put the danger reading at 4.11–4.38:1 over --fab-bg-1 on four of seven themes, and Bone Ash above is corrected to the shipped form.

<EssencePool>

shipped

An essence requirement has no single source: several carriers each contribute, and the player decides which. Every essence threshold on one stage draws from one allocation and one source list, because a carrier is one physical thing — a Duskglass spent here gives its Radiant and its Shadow, and it cannot be spent twice.

two thresholds, one spend — a bar each, a source list once
Shared essence allocation
Radiant4 / 4
Shadow4 / 3
Sunmote+2 Radiant · 3 held · 2 unallocated
Duskglass+1 Radiant · +2 Shadow · 2 held · 0 unallocated
Shade Ink+3 Shadow · 1 held · 1 unallocated
Shadow: 1 more than required
One bar per threshold, one row per carrier, and the carrier row states what it contributes to each pool — +1 Radiant · +2 Shadow — which is the only way a player can plan a spend that satisfies two thresholds at once. Two Duskglass fill Shadow to 4 against a requirement of 3; the overshoot is stated rather than clamped or hidden, because spending a carrier you cannot get back is a real cost the player is choosing. Every increment is disabled once every pool is met, so the control stops the player overspending by accident while still allowing it deliberately from a pool that is still short.
short — the bar carries the entity tint until it is met
Shared essence allocation
Clarity2 / 5
Dewglass+2 Clarity · 4 held · 3 unallocated
Moonpetal+3 Clarity · 1 held · 1 unallocated
While a pool is short its fill is the essence’s own tint and its count is secondary ink; the moment it is met, both turn success. Only a carrier that gives an essence the stage needs is listed, so the source list never carries a row that cannot help.
Canonical spec
  • container a well — bg-1, radius 9, padding 12, its regions 8 apart, the caller’s 9px kicker at 0.08em inside it
  • bar a 26 icon chip at radius 7, the essence name at 11.5px, a mono got / need, and a 6px track named by its N of M value text; bars 4 apart
  • fill the essence tint while short, --fab-success once met; the count follows it
  • source row radius 9 on bg-2, 4 apart · 26 icon chip · name at 11.5px · mono contribution line · a 30 stepper
  • contribution line the caller’s reading: per-essence yield, then held; the Journal adds what is unallocated
  • increment disabled when no stock is spare, or when every pool is already met; under capAtHeld it is disabled only at the held count, so a met pool still takes a deliberate surplus
  • overshoot stated in words beneath the list; never clamped, never silent
Svelte API
  • thresholds {essence, amount, sources[], icon?, tint?, props?}[] — the stage’s essence requirements; repeated essence amounts are summed into one pool before comparing contributions or disabling increments. props is spread on the threshold, so a caller’s hooks stay literal.
  • sources[] {id, label, art?, icon?, tint?, props?, inputProps?} — deduplicated by id across thresholds; props is spread on the carrier row and inputProps onto its Stepper input.
  • allocation {componentId: count} bindable — one per stage, not one per threshold
  • onStep (componentId, delta, next) required
  • yield (componentId, essence) → number — the per-unit contribution
  • spare (componentId) → number — from the stage’s claims map · held (componentId) → number
  • capAtHeld boolean, default false — cap each stepper at held rather than freezing it once every pool is met; crafting passes it, the Journal does not
  • locked boolean · essenceLabel (essence) required · label · hint
  • sourceReading (source, contributions, held, spare) · overshootLabel (essenceLabel, amount) · meterValueLabel (got, need) · allocationLabel, decrementLabel, incrementLabel (source) — every word is the caller’s; each overshoot sentence carries data-essence-overshoot keyed by its essence
  • history optional recorded {totals, labels, requirements, carriers} account. Renders recorded channel totals and one actor-qualified physical carrier row with all of its contributions; no allocation controls, held stock, editable progress or steppers. Absence retains the active allocation form.
Why the allocation is keyed to the stage and not to the requirement. Model a spend per threshold and the same Duskglass can be allocated to Radiant and to Shadow independently, which lets a player satisfy both from one carrier they only own once. One allocation shared across every threshold on the stage is the only shape in which the arithmetic is honest, and it is why the source list is rendered once rather than repeated under each bar. Under a routed recipe the allocation is keyed by stage and route, because changing route changes what the stage is asking for.
This refines the chooser family rather than replacing it. Active allocation retains its shared pool. A historical account uses history, not disabled active controls: a channelled total and a source list once, with no invented live stock. Issue 1648 adds the second independent consumer, HistoricalRunDetail, beside StepDetails; issue 1644 adds crafting’s EssencePoolPanel as an adapter that keeps its own “Your selection” recap beneath the pool.
Measured at issue 1644; shipped at issue 2457 (maintainer, 2026-10-12). Issue 1644 measured the rendered pool on player-crafting-essence-pool-shared, player-crafting-essence-overshoot and fabricate-journal-lifecycle-essence-shared, and issue 2403 redraws this specimen to it: the kicker 9px at 0.08em inside the well, the bars 4px apart, a carrier name at 11.5px and the comfortable stepper 30px tall. The icon chips were measured at radius 9; issue 1523 later put the 26 Medallion on its rung’s radius 7, which is what ships and what is drawn. DEBT: the kicker, the hint and the overshoot ship in --fab-text-subtle at 3.54–3.98:1 on --fab-bg-1, and the carrier reading at 3.34–3.78:1 on --fab-bg-2, in six themes; they are drawn in --fab-text-muted, and issue 2368 owns them.

<RunProgress> <StageNav> <StageCard>

RunProgress · shippedStageNav · shippedStageCard · shipped

A staged run is read one stage at a time. A track per stage says where the run is, a windowed numbered nav says which stage you are looking at, and exactly one stage — the one being worked — carries live controls. Every other stage is inert and says only what it knows.

progress — one track per stage, filled, part-filled, empty
Progress
Tracks tile the width so the number of stages is legible without counting: a full track is a finished stage, the part-filled one is the stage being served, and empty tracks are stages not reached. The stage in progress takes the accent; finished stages take success. The line beside the kicker is reserved for a blocker and is otherwise empty — the countdown belongs to the time card and the state to the stage tag, so this line only ever states the one thing no other surface says.
stage nav — a five-stage window over a longer run
Viewing stage 3 of 8
At most five numerals are rendered and the window follows the stage being viewed, so an eight-stage run does not turn its nav into a second list. The arrows dim at the ends and never hide, matching the pagination rule. Two marks, two facts: the selected numeral is filled accent, and the stage actually being worked keeps an accent border wherever it sits in the window. Once the two diverge a Return to current stage N control appears, because a player who has read ahead needs one press to return to the thing they can act on.

The worked stage states its output only; what it consumes is the live slot row below, and saying it in both places invites the two to disagree. The body sits behind a full-bleed hairline so the record half and the control half of the card are separable at a glance. Every region takes one 12px inset, 12 apart, and the output is the four-column truncated ListRow grid.

Every stage that is not being worked drops to a dashed frame on no fill and carries no control at all — a player is never asked to choose out of turn. An unreached stage states what only it knows: the time it will need, the check it will roll, and the shape of any open slot. A finished stage becomes a record, its numeral a success tick and what it consumed and produced the same four-column rows the worked stage’s output uses, so a run reads as its own log without a second surface.
Canonical spec
  • tracks 6px, radius 999, a 1px --fab-border on --fab-surface-raised, tiled by grid-auto-flow:column at --fab-space-chip — one per stage, no visible label, each a progressbar named by its stage
  • nav 26 numerals at radius 7, window of 5, arrows dim at the ends
  • stage card radius 9 — bg-2 with a hairline when worked, transparent and dashed when not
  • numeral 24 round, mono 11; a tick when done, a pause glyph when held
  • tag a 999 pill, success for Your move, warning for Paused, absent otherwise
  • regions one 12px inset: the card pads 12 above and below and sets its regions 12 apart, and the heading, io, facts, note and body each pad 12 on either side; the facts and the body sit below a full-bleed hairline with 12 above them, and a fact after the first takes its own hairline 4 above it
  • io each group the card’s full width, its items the four-column truncated dense ListRow grid, 4 apart
  • inks its summary, note, fact label, inactive name and io quantity in --fab-text-muted, and its inactive numeral (on --fab-surface-active) in --fab-text-secondary, all at 4.5:1 or more in every theme (issue 2353); StageNav’s numerals and position line ink --fab-text-muted
RunProgress API
  • Read from RunProgress.svelte’s $props() at issue 1644.
  • stages the run’s stage list — a stage whose status is done or succeeded, or that sits before current, fills its track · current index — the stage being worked
  • progress 0–100 — the current stage’s own fill
  • label the kicker, which names the track group when drawn · ariaLabel — the group’s name when no kicker is drawn
  • blocker string — the one line beside the Progress kicker
  • No events and no rest spread; the tracks, their group and their stage-named progress roles are <StageBars>’, and an unnamed stage of several is labelled “Stage n of m” here, through the FABRICATE.Common.StageBars.Unnamed key, while a named stage of several reads “p%, stage n of m”, p its whole percent truncated, as its bar’s valueText, through the FABRICATE.Common.StageBars.Position key; a lone stage takes neither.
StageNav API
  • Read from StageNav.svelte’s $props() at issue 1644.
  • stages the run’s stage list · current index — the stage being worked
  • view bindable — the stage being read, local to the surface
  • window number = 5, clamped to 1–5 · onView (index)
  • stageLabel (stage, index) — each numeral’s accessible name, since the numeral is a bare number; it defaults to the number
  • previousLabel · nextLabel — the arrows’ names · positionLabel (view, count) — the nav’s name and its Viewing stage n of m line · returnLabel (current) — the Return to current stage N text
  • Fewer than two stages render nothing; no rest spread.
StageCard API
  • Read from StageCard.svelte’s $props() at issue 1644.
  • stage {name, summary, status} · index · current boolean
  • state past | current | future | paused | failed | done — paused draws the pause glyph and the warning tag
  • tag {label, tone} | null — absent while a stage is simply serving time
  • facts {id, icon, label, value}[] — rendered for a stage that is not current
  • body (stage) snippet — rendered for the worked stage only
  • stage.status when supplied owns the completion marker independently of browse position; failed or unexecuted stages never acquire a success checkmark from state="past".
  • showHeading boolean = true — a single-stage surface may suppress the redundant numeral/name header while retaining the stage body
  • showNumber boolean = true — a single stage retains its captured purpose heading while omitting the redundant numbered marker.
  • io {kind, label, items, emptyText, content?}[] - paired inert input/output groups of dense ListRow, before facts and the current-only body. Optional content is a read-only snippet replacing plain items, used for future alternatives and route/ladder outputs within the same pairing. Items carry name, img/art, icon, tint and caller-formatted quantityText; a label-only item remains readable. Current shows Produces only; past shows Consumed/Produced; future shows Will consume/Will produce. Each group takes the card’s full width at its 12px inset, the groups 12 apart.
  • presentation active | history, default active — history has the filled radius-9 recap, never current controls or a browse-state dashed shell. A failed recap takes the danger edge. Every attempted stage renders together; unattempted stages have no recap.
  • note optional inert looking-back/ahead sentence beneath the facts, in 10.5px subtle ink.
  • output() optional preview snippet at the same 12px inset, above the live control separator, for routed or progressive output compositions that need more than entry chips.
  • No events and no rest spread.
view is not current, and neither is derived from the other. Reading ahead must not advance the run, and completing a stage must not strand the player on a stage they were inspecting. The surface therefore holds two indices: the run owns current, the component owns view, and the Return to current stage N control exists precisely because they can diverge. Both are keyed by run id and held in the component, not lifted into the run store — every completion refreshes that store, and a view index held there would snap the player away mid-read.
Measured at issue 1644: StageNav ships; RunProgress and StageCard ship at issue 2257. StageNav, on past-stage and future-stage, matches its canonical spec: 26 numerals and arrows at radius 7 a gap of 4 apart, the selected numeral filled accent, the worked one keeping its accent border, both arrows disabled at the ends and never hidden, and a 26px Return to current stage N control once view and current diverge, whose weight and ink are <Button>’s. RunProgress, on past-stage, draws 6px tracks at radius 999 tiled at --fab-space-chip, success then accent, under the shipped <Kicker>, which it adopted at issue 2257 because its hand-rolled subtle kicker measured under the 4.5:1 floor. StageCard, on its five override frames, matches radius 9, the bg-2 hairline and the dashed inactive frame, the 24 round mono-11 numeral with its tick and pause glyph, and the 999 tag, whose padding, size and edge are <Chip>’s density="list", recorded against that entry. Re-measured at issue 2257, its regions sit at one 12px inset, which issue 1648 chose over the 48px indent, and its io is the four-column truncated ListRow grid; the specimen is redrawn to both (D22). Its 10.5px summary, note and fact label, its inactive 12px/600 name, and its io rows’ quantity ink --fab-text-muted, and its inactive 11px numeral (on --fab-surface-active) inks --fab-text-secondary, because muted measures 4.36:1 there in fabricate; StageNav’s numerals and position line ink --fab-text-muted (issue 2353).

<YieldScale> <OutcomeLadder>

YieldScale · shippedOutcomeLadder · shipped

What a gathering run might bring back, and afterwards where the roll landed. A drop table is one roll read against an ordered scale, so it is stated in that order — commonest first — rather than as a list of independent chances. A preview whose reward selection reads authored rank, the gathering find list, keeps that rank instead.

before the roll — the scale, commonest first
Possible yields
Greyfell Scree

×3 100%
Iron Nodule

×2 70%
Silver Seam
Effective roll 71 or higher
×1 30%
Skyfall Shard
Effective roll 96 or higher
×1 5%
A find comes back when the effective roll reaches its threshold, so a higher roll reaches further down the scale — and stating the rows in descending chance is what makes that legible before anything is rolled. Each row says the effective roll it needs, the engine’s own threshold, rather than leaving the player to infer the comparison; the task’s modifier and any situational bonus move the roll, never the threshold, so no chance is stated as certain. A find at 100% takes the success pill; everything else is neutral, because a percentage is not good news until it is compared with a number that does not exist yet. A preview states authored order where reward selection reads it: gathering reward selection is by authored row order, so the find list passes order="authored" and each chance stays its row’s figure rather than its position.
after the roll — the same scale, cut once
Where the roll landed
Greyfell Scree

×3 100%

×2 70%
Rolled 41Anything rarer than this fell short

One roll, so one cut. The record keeps the whole scale and draws the line where the roll fell: rows above it cleared it and turn success, rows below are dashed and dimmed and say what they needed. The near miss is the point — a record that listed only what came back would throw away the one fact that tells a player whether to go back to this site. Two edge cases carry their own note: a roll short of every threshold puts the line at the top, and a roll that reaches all of them puts it at the bottom reading every find on the scale cleared it.
legacy history — recorded row rolls, no global cut

If Gem recorded an effective roll of 98, show it after Rolled 94. An unknown outcome stays neutral; an unknown quantity changes only its quantity label. The known Ore ×2 stays visible. Unattributed actual receipts appear once below, never repeating Ore's represented receipt.
routed by check — the whole ladder, failure included

Where the roll lands is what the run yields, so the ladder is stated whole and in order, each tier with the band that selects it. Failure is a tier like any other — a danger frame and an empty yield list saying what nothing means — not a separate case bolted on beneath. The ladder belongs to the system rather than to the run, so this surface reports it and never edits it.
after a successful roll — the one tier it reached
FruitfulYour roll14–19

Once a roll resolves, the tier it routed through says so: an accent edge and a Your roll pill beside its name, two signals rather than colour alone. Exactly one tier carries it — a row merged from several authored tiers carries it for any of them — and a failed roll marks none. Before a roll nothing is marked.
Canonical spec
  • order descending chance by default — the scale is one comparison, not a set of them; authored keeps entry order where rank is authored, and draws no cut
  • row the selectable ListRow form, radius 9 on bg-1 with a 4 8 inset · borderless 26 icon chip · 12/600 name over its 10.5 reading · mono quantity · borderless list-density chance pill · one flex line (bodyBasis="fill")
  • cleared success wash and border, its reading and pill in the secondary ink · missed dashed border, an untinted glyph, subtle name
  • cut a list-density accent chip carrying the roll, a 1px accent rule, and a note naming what the line means
  • perRow the dense ListRow · a 22px bordered medallion (1px --fab-border, radius 6, bg-3) whose glyph takes the row’s tint, else accent, at the medallion’s 0.9rem default · a 12/600 name whose growth pushes the reading toward a mono quantity · a bordered list-density chance chip · a cleared row on the success wash and border, its reading and chip in the secondary ink
  • tier radius 9, a tinted head carrying a 10px glyph, the name and a bare mono band in the secondary ink (danger on a failing tier), yields as 24px radius-6 chips that wrap, their name and ×N on one baseline, each led by a centred 14px picture or 9px glyph
  • No control anywhere in either — both are records, and the roll is fired from the action bar
Svelte API
  • entries {id, name, icon, tint, qty, chance}[] — sorted by the component, not the caller
  • order chance (default) | authored — authored keeps entry order and draws no cut
  • roll number | null — a recorded shared number permits the cut when all outcomes are known
  • rollModel shared (default) | perRow | unknown — only shared permits a cut; row-only history uses labels.evidence for each row's recorded fields
  • tiers {id, ids?, name, band?, fail, emptyText?, yields[], props?, bandProps?, reachedProps?}[] — the ladder form; a tier with no band draws no band; each props object lands on the tier, its band or its pill as a caller’s hooks
  • yields {id?, name, art|img, icon, tint, quantity, detail, props?}[] — each a chip led by its picture where resolveCraftingArt finds art, else its glyph; a name ellipsizes with its full name as its title; a group’s name, at 600, keeps its full width while its members wrap at whitespace beside it; and props land on the chip
  • emptyTierText required — a failing tier says what nothing means in the product’s words
  • reachedId string | null · reachedLabel — the first tier whose ids, else its id, contain the id carries the labelled pill and data-outcome-rolled; null marks none
  • label · hint — the kicker and its sentence above the tiers · successLabel · failureLabel — a visually hidden name for each tier’s status glyph, so pass and fail are not carried by the glyph alone · class plus a rest spread on the root, after the class
Issue 1648 result-row override. YieldScale’s perRow evidence rows stay dense ListRows with a 22px Medallion, the name and its recorded fields inline, and a bordered chance chip; shared cuts and descending chance ordering retain their default behavior, and order="authored" opts out of both. OutcomeLadder retains tier headings, bands and empty-tier text, and takes each result’s art/img and caller-formatted quantity onto its chip. Neither turns previews into actual awards. Issue 1644 draws crafting’s routed tiers and salvage’s routed body through the same ladder, where it marks the one tier a roll reached and a band is optional.
The YieldScale entry contract. YieldScale: entries=[{id,name,art?,icon?,tint?,qty?,chance,cleared?: boolean|null,rawRoll?,effectiveRoll?,threshold?}], roll=null, rollModel='shared', order='chance', labels={}, label='', hint=''. rollModel accepts shared, perRow and unknown. order accepts chance (descending, the default) and authored: entry order, for a preview whose rank is authored, with no cut; a known shared roll then stays a standalone reading. Only shared permits a global cut or the default comparison when cleared is absent. Historical perRow shows each recorded raw roll and effective roll when different, with independently known threshold, outcome and actual quantity; equal row rolls never establish sharing. Explicit null outcomes stay neutral. Optional labels.evidence(entry) owns the recorded sentence; the default callbacks remain threshold, cleared, missed, quantity, chance, cut, topCutNote, bottomCutNote and cutNote. Unknown amounts do not hide known neighboring amounts. Issue #1648 extends the entry contract; rendered acceptance remains pending.
Why this is not a table. A table earns its shape where a reader compares the same field down a column and would want to sort it. Here the order is the meaning: sorting this by name would destroy the only thing the scale says. Each row also carries art, a sentence and a pill, which is a list row’s job. Section 09’s table rule routes it here.
Shared roll, stated once. Explicit shared-root records retain one cut. The approved legacy exception uses per-row rolls with no global cut when only row evidence was recorded; neither the first row nor equal row values prove a shared roll. Each row retains its known fields even when a neighbor has missing evidence.
Both converge on the specimen at issue 2257 (ruling 2026-10-07; D7 as amended 2026-10-10, D14, D15, D19, D20). YieldScale’s rows outside perRow set the reading under the name beside a borderless 26px mark, on one flex line through ListRow’s opt-in bodyBasis="fill", with a borderless chance pill and the shared Kicker; the gathering find list states the engine’s own threshold again, as Effective roll N or higher. The row text, the pill, the roll marker and the preview’s sentences are redrawn here to what ships: a one-line row measures the shared row, about 44px, and a wrapped sentence adds whole lines. OutcomeLadder draws a 10px head glyph, the band as bare mono text and the yields as 24px wrapping chips; its band and chip inks are the secondary ink, redrawn from the specimen’s subtle, which measures under 4.5:1 on the success head (D13). Sets & groups

The container layer above the row. An ingredient set holds what a craft consumes; a result set holds what it produces. A recipe may carry several of each, and the resolution mode decides which set routes to which result set.

The two sets

prose

A SET is the parent container. An ingredient set holds what a craft consumes; a result set holds what it produces. Both hold the same two elements — picker rows and choice groups — and differ only in which kinds their rows offer.

A choice group here is the player choosing their reward.
The rows are the same component. A set contains <PickerRow> and <ChoiceGroup> — there is no separate result row. What changes between the two sets is the role the set carries, which restricts the kinds the row’s select offers: requirement kinds on the ingredient side, result kinds on the result side. Everything else about the row is identical, which is why the two sides never drift.

Both sets are renameable. The name is the first control in the card, because it is what every other surface refers to the set by — a routing select, a validation message, a tier assignment. An unnamed set is addressable only by position, which is what makes a reordered list dangerous.

Routed by ingredients

prose

The set the crafter satisfies decides the result set. Each set names exactly one result set; several sets may name the same one.

It lives on the recipe’s Overview tab and answers “what does this recipe actually do?” in one screen: every source, its target, and where two sources share one. A GM re-points routing here without opening a set, which is the common edit; the set card below is where a set’s contents are authored, which is the rarer one. Both write the same field, so neither is a copy of the other.

Every row reserves the same trailing column, so the select sits at one position down the list and a shared marker never moves it. Sets B and C both produce Plain blade, and each says so, because a GM changing that set is changing it for both.

Neither mode routes: one ingredient set, one success group, and nothing to assign. What they add is a second group selected by role rather than by any mapping — the results a failed check awards, where the system allows results on failure.

These two are selected by role and never by index or name, so neither carries a source list, neither can be assigned to anything, and neither is renameable — a rename would change nothing, because nothing refers to them by name. The lock glyph says which sets those are. The Failure set is optional: absent, or authored and left empty, a failed check produces nothing. The toggle is the opt-in. Turning it on adds the empty role: 'failure' group and turning it off removes it, so the group’s presence is the only record of the choice and nothing is drawn while it is absent; where the system’s failure-result policy forbids results on failure the toggle cannot add the group, says why and links to the Checks Studio, and a group already present can still be removed. Validation counts only the non-failure group toward “exactly one success group”, so carrying a failure group never makes a simple recipe invalid.

A group name may not be a reserved failure keyword — fail, failure, miss, none and their siblings — because the routed modes match an outcome against those words, and a group borrowing one would be selected by the failure path rather than by its tier. Progressive has no reserved failure group at all.

What each mode allows

prose

The three modes these surfaces route between. progressive and alchemy are real modes with their own shapes — progressive notably awards every result set whose threshold the roll meets, rather than selecting one — and are specified in the resolution-modes capability rather than here.

Mode Ingredient sets Result sets Routing key
Simpleexactly oneone success, plus an optional reserved failure setnone
Routed by ingredientsone or moreone or morethe set the crafter satisfies
Routed by checkone or moreone or morethe check outcome tier — check required
Changing mode can strip work: a recipe with more than one set or group cannot become Simple without losing them, so the editor states what will be deleted before the switch rather than after.

Screen recipes

This app has four screen archetypes — browse, editor, player and validation. Build from the recipe down, not from the parts up. A settings screen is an editor without a breadcrumb or a back-and-save pair, because it edits a scope rather than a record.

A · Browse screen

prose

A list of records you can filter, sort, page, select and open. Recipes, components, essences, settlements, businesses, parties — all the same screen.

Order is fixed
  • AppTitleBar · NavSidebar · page header with one primary action · FilterBar · list · Pagination

Rules
  • Row state is a StatusButton, never a Toggle.
  • The pagination bar sits outside the scroll area so it never moves.
  • Filter, sort and page state live in an app store — never a URL.
  • An inspector rail is optional here; it belongs to the editor screen.

Order is fixed
  • NavSidebar icon rail · browse column with search and filters · detail pane
  • The detail pane leads with its identity header, then progress, then requirements. The header carries at most one primary action: zero is correct, two never is.
  • A run in flight extends the same order: identity and the run action bar, the notice region, the verdict where one exists, progress — tracks, stage nav, the worked stage — then yields, then the record.
  • The browse column may carry two fixed regions — runs in flight above, finished below — each scrolling internally with its pager outside the scroll area, so the finished region keeps the bottom of the column as the active list grows.
Rules
  • No premium signal, in any state — no badge, no padlocked entry, no teaser tab, no upgrade offer. Canon is absolute on this, and it is why <PremiumPanel> and Locked.upgrade left the set.
  • The player never authors a group — every requirement chooser is a read-only mirror of the GM's group; a reward whose chooser is the player is picked at award time, through the chooser's award face.
  • Craft is one primary action per pane. Everything else is quiet.
  • One primary action per stage, not per pane per session — pause, cancel and the completion switch are bordered secondaries at the same height.
  • The world clock is stated and never operated here. A run may be set to finish on its own; it then carries a bolt so the player knows which runs move without them.

prose

Every editor has one, and it is the same screen every time: a verdict, the counts, then the issues grouped by the part of the record they belong to. A GM who has read one has read all of them.
